questions.stem: A physician becomes angry at her 80-year-old patient for not following his diet; her own father died of heart failure after ignoring similar advice. What is happening?
questions.explanation: The physician's unconscious reaction stems from her own past. A, B: Transference is the patient's reaction to the physician. C: Denial is a patient defense. E: Paternalism is deciding for the patient.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 37, 46

questions.stem: Which model has the physician explain options and help the patient clarify their own values before choosing?
questions.explanation: The interpretive model elucidates the patient's values and helps select matching interventions. B: The physician decides. C: The physician informs; the patient chooses alone. D: The physician guides toward the best health values as a teacher/friend. E: A practice style, not one of the four models.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 15–16

questions.stem: Which factor does the lecture link to a patient not adhering to the treatment plan?
questions.explanation: Patients with negative transference feel excessive resentment or anger when their expectations aren't met and may not adhere to the treatment plan. A, B, D, E: The lecture states adherence is not related to gender, religion, socioeconomic or marital status, race, intelligence, or education.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 36–37

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl involved in an accident won't say her name. What should the physician do?

options.A: Repeat the question using direct closed questions
options.B: Ask her questions in the third person
options.C: Avoid speaking with her until a parent arrives
options.D: Tell her that nothing bad will happen to her
options.E: Ask open-ended questions about the accident

questions.explanation: For young children the lecture recommends questions in the third person and non-verbal means such as drawing together. A: Repeating direct questions doesn't help a child who won't answer. C: Waiting delays communication. D: Falsely reassuring statements are inappropriate. E: Open-ended questions suit adults who speak freely; the slide's child-specific techniques are third-person questions and drawing.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 32, 45

questions.stem: In a two-person conversation, roughly how much of the social meaning is carried by non-verbal components?
questions.explanation: Non-verbal cues (eye contact, posture, voice, proximity) carry ≥65%; verbal content carries <35%. A, B, C, D: Too low.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slide 29

questions.stem: A patient is overly talkative and keeps drifting to unrelated topics. Which interviewing technique does the lecture recommend?

options.D: Remaining silent until the patient stops

questions.explanation: Direct questions elicit information quickly in an emergency or when the patient is seductive or overly talkative. A: Open-ended questions encourage free speech, the opposite of what's needed here. C, E: Techniques for young children. D: Silence lets the digression continue.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 31–32

questions.stem: A competent 60-year-old's biopsy shows cancer. His adult children ask the physician to tell them first and let them relay the news. What does the lecture say?

options.A: Tell the children, who know him best
options.B: Tell him only the diagnosis, not the prognosis
options.C: Reassure him that the result is probably nothing serious
options.D: Refer him to a psychiatrist to deliver the news
options.E: Tell him directly and completely about diagnosis and prognosis

questions.explanation: Adult patients are generally told the complete truth about diagnosis and prognosis, directly and not relayed through relatives. A: Information is not relayed through relatives. B: The truth should be complete. C: Falsely reassuring statements are inappropriate. D: The treating physician is responsible; referral is for medical problems outside his range.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slide 30
